utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. A special warm welcome today to everybody when we start now this 100th day of the trial, Prosecutor versus Dr. Stakic. And I would give up my job in case we would ever read on the LiveNote Day 200. So please, let's take care that we speed up a little bit. This case is a very problematic day. Yesterday, I announced that we would sit in the morning. Later on, we heard it was not possible. And you know even better than the Judges did, we only learned at 6.00 in the evening that we would sit today in the afternoon. A number of changes have occurred. This is one reason that Judge Vassylenko is not present in the moment, for personal reasons. May I ask before starting the parties and the accused, Dr. Stakic, in person, whether they agree that for the first portion, that means the first 90 minutes, we sit under Rule 15 bis in the composition of the two of us. Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we have no objection. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We don't have any objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. This was the first step. Second step: The bureau meeting scheduled, rescheduled, now scheduled again will definitely take place as from 6.00 today. So therefore, we have to stop on or about 6.00 this evening. As regards tomorrow, it was my intention, and I emphasize "intention" that we could enable that all the witnesses waiting this week could be heard, and therefore it would be possible to start in the morning and we would have Courtroom I during the entire day. I know that there could be a conflict with the interests of the parties, especially the Defence having to discuss issues sometimes with the client and with upcoming witnesses. Therefore, could you please give me a hint what is absolutely mandatory for you, what is the framework in which we can hear the case tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. We would like to if at all possible keep the framework consistent with that which was outlined to us previously, that is that we proceed tomorrow afternoon at 2.15, and conclude with the witness that we expect to call either starting this afternoon and/or tomorrow, and then we'll proceed next week as outlined and scheduled by the Court. We cannot and would not like to proceed tomorrow the entire day from 9.00 to 6.00 or whatever it was envisioned for a number of reasons; namely, because we would like to meet with Dr. Stakic to go over some issues with the witness that's upcoming for next week, who is here. Also, based upon information and belief, and personal knowledge, the witness that is upcoming has some documents that we are photocopying that we would use as evidence, and in all fairness to the OTP, we would like to give them a couple of days so that they could review those documents and have them translated so that they could have a better understanding as opposed to spring it on them during his testimony. Likewise, we're going to offer those documents to the Court in advance, as well as prepare a more detailed proffer as we have, in my opinion, with the witness that is following the present one who is on the stand. Next, if I may, with the Court's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I can understand. Only to be on the safe side, it is your submission it would be impossible, for example, to start tomorrow at 1.00?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And work until when Your Honour, if I may inquire?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: From 1.00 until 7.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Based upon my conversations with our client, it would be not impossible, but it would certainly be taxing on him as well as on the attorneys. We do believe that it would not be practical because we think we could finish the witness that will be starting following this witness this afternoon, and it may take, based upon what the Prosecution has told me, that we may be able to finish that one particular witness by tomorrow. We will endeavour to do that. So just so that we're clear: There are two remaining witnesses, one that is on the stand, and it's my understanding from the Prosecution, as he informed me yesterday, that he may take a couple of hours with him. And then the following witness, based on our proffer and the amended proffer that we submitted to the Court, we have approximately three hours with that witness, and we can only envision and speculate that the OTP would likewise have a couple of hours at the least. So keeping that in mind, we would hope, and we will work towards completing that witness. But the final witness, we will commence next week, who is here, depending again on the schedule as we discussed, of Mrs. Balaban, who is coming, as well as Dr. Mujadzic, who is also coming on Monday. So we will work around that and prepare the appropriate proffer for that witness. So if the Court insists and feels there is a necessity, we can meet at 1.00, and we will proceed as long as it takes to conclude that one witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So I then want to ask Madam Registrar to find out whether it's possible in order to, in a way of compromise, to start at 1.30 up until 7.00, aiming at concluding the next witness tomorrow. You had another issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If I may, Your Honour. I'm not sure if it's the appropriate time, yesterday in our 65 ter (i) conference, we did discuss numerous things such as the plea agreement and the factual backdrop of the plea agreement involving Biljana Plavsic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I just interrupt. This was really a preliminary discussion. Before we really go into details, I would like that the case be called when we know now that we can proceed under 15 bis. May I ask you, please, to call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon. This is Case Number IT-97-24-T, the Prosecutor versus Milomir Stakic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. And the appearances, for the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Nicholas Koumjian, Mike McVicker, and Ruth Karper for the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Branko Lukic and John Ostojic for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ostojic, you may proceed now please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It's a minor point. I would just once again in connection with the issue of Biljana Plavsic, we would like as we suggested yesterday that we be given the tapes so that our client can also review them in the language in which he understands, as prescribed in the Rules before this Tribunal. Secondly, on the disclosure of the typewritten notes from the transcripts, specifically disclosure 1268, it states on the very first page, and quite honestly, we haven't completed our review of those transcripts, but on the very first page of that disclosure, which is the first tape of Biljana Plavsic's interview of June 22nd, 2001, that she in fact had another interview --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I think we did agree that these -- that the Defence was bound by nondisclosure on the tapes. And I don't know that anything secret is going to be stated. But perhaps -- or is that there is anything secret. But perhaps we should go into private session just for a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Closed session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good afternoon. We are continuing your testimony of yesterday. Today you are still under solemn declaration, as you know. Yesterday I asked you to rethink and maybe even to review yesterday's statement, and I told you that I would ask you in the beginning whether or not you have to make some changes or amendments.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. In connection with my testimony yesterday, and my answers to the questions asked by the Defence, everything that I said corresponds with the events as they happened in the municipality and the town of Prijedor within the time frame the questions refer to. As I pointed out yesterday, I am able to corroborate the testimony I offered with documents. Furthermore, I am fully aware that when one speaks about documents, most of the documents were taken away from the municipal files in Prijedor and are currently here in the possession of the Tribunal. I also know that in view of the fact that in my opinion, due to the peculiar nature of my tasks in 1992, the documents are many, and the list of documents is very comprehensive. If needed, I should be willing to offer assistance to the Honourable Chamber in tracking these documents down. In my opinion, this is an activity that may be defined in a way as lex specialis. On the other hand, we are talking about documents that must be placed within their historical context; namely, during the implementation of tasks on which I worked as a member of the institution where I worked, there were a number of documents that had been adopted one year before 1992. The implementation of the decisions contained in those documents ensued in 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry, might I interrupt you at this point in time. But this will be subject to the upcoming questions both by the Defence and the OTP. My question was only whether or not you wanted to correct, amend, or change in whole or in part yesterday's testimony and from you have stated now, I think your answer is no, there is nothing to change or nothing to amend and nothing to correct. Is this correct? We're not speaking about any anonymous documents; we are speaking about your concrete testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, probably, there might have to be additions, but I was trying to be as succinct, as precise as possible in my testimony yesterday, and I think I have succeeded. So I think in answer to your question about my testimony yesterday, I have no further changes to make.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. We will come back to this during the question and answers. The only thing I want to ask you, if it would be possible for you to speak a little bit faster, it would help us all. Thank you. The floor is yours for the Defence, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Dragic, again.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I don't have many questions to ask you today. I would like to start with the following. The question I'm about to ask you is related to your position at work. Did you ever dismiss anyone, and did people stop reporting for work in your organisation? So we are talking about the period after the takeover on the 30th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As concerns the organisation where I worked during the specified period, there were 22 persons, 22 employees working there. The ethnic makeup of those employees was that there were both Croats -- there were Croats, Serbs, and Muslims, all three ethnic groups. The section of the organisation of which I was the head, not a single employee, regardless of his or her nationality, was fired or anything like that. All the more; I tried to be as understanding towards employees of the other nationalities, and I tried to grant their individual requests to be replaced. Correction, to exchange property. And I'm talking about exchange of property between property situated in Croatia and property situated in Bosnia-Herzegovina. We are talking about Prijedor Municipality and the Municipality of Rijeka in the Republic of Croatia. At this time, people started not showing up for work. But all of my employees, the employees of the section in which I was the head, would call me on the phone and tell me that they were carrying out preparations to leave Prijedor Municipality and asked to have their documents ready for them, their personal documents which were kept in their personal file so that they could come and pick their documents up. The departure of non-Serbian employees was happening successively within a single period; it didn't happen all at once. Not all non-Serbs left the institution. They worked the same way in 1992 as they still work today. So by way of conclusion, as head of that particular organisation, I never blackmailed, threatened, or fired anyone. And all of the employees can confirm this, even those who no longer work there, and also those who still work there. So much for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know anything about the attempt to remove Dr. Stakic from his position as the president of the Municipal Assembly? Do you know when this started? Do you know who took part in it, and what the reasons were for this attempt to remove him? Do you know anything related to that?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do know that - I think it was during the last three months of 1992 - there were certain activities aimed at an attempt to remove Dr. Stakic from his position as the president of the Municipal Assembly, and this was prepared among the ranks of the SDS, the Serbian Democratic Party. The rumour had it, and we all heard it through the grapevine, because it was a much talked about thing in the town at that time, that within the party itself, there were younger people making their way up who, to put it in simple terms, only cared about power, obtaining power. The arguments that were offered at this time to have Dr. Stakic removed from his position as the president of the Municipal Assembly were that Dr. Stakic was first and foremost not even a member of that party. As far as I can remember, those were the intentions of a particular faction within the SDS, and they were successful in achieving their aim. Dr. Stakic was indeed removed from his position. And I also believe - we are talking about the beginning of 1993 - that Dr. Stakic then resigned formally in writing, before he was finally relieved of his duty at the next session of the assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now I would like to address a different event. Do you know anything about the circumstances surrounding the signing of the Lisbon agreement, and do you know anything Mr. Alija Izetbegovic's role in that at the time the agreement was signed, and for several days after that, and do you know what exactly the Lisbon agreement entailed?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember the agreement, superficially, perhaps I should add. I know that there was talk of mediation by the international community to help bring an end to the crisis in the Yugoslav Federation. The international community had an active role in this. I know there was a conference in Lisbon, and as a result of the conference and the agreement reached in Lisbon, a conference attended also by Mr. Alija Izetbegovic, the then president of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Alija Izetbegovic signed the document and thereby gave his consent for Bosnia-Herzegovina to remain within Yugoslavia. After this information was published by the media, within the municipality itself, the Serbs rejoiced. Serbs in the municipality were happy that a political agreement was reached. However, their joy was shortlived. Very soon, a day or two later, Mr. Izetbegovic said, and this also appeared in the media, that his signature in Lisbon was null and void. The media also said that Mr. Alija Izetbegovic had given up on the Lisbon agreement because he had come under pressure from the American administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much for this elucidation. I only have one further question, and we are shifting again to a totally different area. I will ask you about the clash in Kozarac. Did any of the -- did any of the people who were not locals get killed in Kozarac during that particular incident because of, for example, their skin colour?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in connection with the events in Kozarac in 1992, people did talk about it in the town. It was said that the soldiers who were in that area, in the immediate vicinity at the junction of the Prijedor/Banja Luka main road where you turn off to go to Kozarac, a uniformed person was noticed; the body of a uniformed person lying dead on the ground. The skin colour was black, as the Bosnians would say, it was the a black man. So you could assume that in addition to the local people, the Green Berets were also aided by foreign mercenaries during the operation in Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Dragic. This concludes the examination-in-chief by the Defence. Now I'll hand you over to the OTP and finally to the Honourable Chamber. Once again, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Mr. Koumjian, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Dragic, for coming and offering us your insights into the events preceding and following the takeover of Prijedor on the 30th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Could the usher please move the ELMO back so I could have a direct line of sight.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, have you ever seen a dead body that has been lying in the sun, in warm weather, for a few days?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: You're not aware of any changes in skin colour following death and decomposition of human remains, are you?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not familiar with that, but what I have just said was that the -- some soldiers who got there immediately after the killing, some 10 minutes after the killing, that's what they said, and they said that the colour of the skin of that body was black. But not only the skin colour, but also the physiognomy and the way the person looked. The person looked like somebody whose skin colour is black and not white.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you for adding that information. I want to move on from that to another subject. Just the facts that you've talked about, the information that you provided, I just want to go over with you how you obtained that information, the basis for this testimony. First I want to start with media. Can you tell the Court, during the period of 1992, did you follow media concerning events in Prijedor specifically, that is, were you able to watch any television, listen to any radio, or read any newspapers that reported on events in Prijedor during that time period?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the access to the media was free. The area of Prijedor could receive television programmes from Croatia, from Bosnia, and for a certain period of time, we could also receive programmes from Belgrade. As far as the radio programmes were concerned, we could even hear broader broadcasts than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. I wasn't very precise in my question. Let me just ask you. Thank you for that information. Specifically, what information did you have? Did you watch Croatian television, for example? Did you read any newspapers regarding events in Prijedor and what newspapers, media, were you exposed to that helped you gather information about political events and other events taking place in the municipality?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have already told you that I personally, as we could do it before the war, we could also do it during the war, that it was one's personal choice what TV station would one watch. One could watch Television Zagreb 1, 2, and 3, and for a short period of time we could also --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I understand we're trying. But my question is not what one could watch; it's what you watched and what you read. Let me be very specific. Did you read Glas newspaper during this time period?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't read Glas. I didn't read it before the war, during the war, or after the war. And I watched all the television programmes. I watched them before the war, I watched them during the war, and I still watch them to this very day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you read Kozarski Vjesnik newspaper during 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, not very often, but yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did you listen to Radio Prijedor during that time period?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very rarely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay, thank you, sir. Also, can you tell the Judges what positions you held in the government or in political life in Prijedor that gave you insight into events such as the takeover of the Serbian -- of the municipality of Prijedor on the 30th of April?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that yesterday. Before the 30th of April, I was the secretary for economics and social affairs in Prijedor Municipality, or to be more precise, I was a member of the Executive Board of the municipality of Prijedor. According to the internal organisation of work, of state organs, or administrative organs, the secretariat that I headed belonged to the Executive Board.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, who exactly took power on the 30th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The army and the reserve police force participated in the takeover. However, during the period of time when this was happening, the orders came from the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: So you're telling us that it was the army that planned and prepared and carried out the takeover. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, isn't it true that the SDS party planned, prepared, and carried out the takeover of Prijedor with the help of the army and police?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was rather the other way around. The army was the one who conducted consultations, and the SDS as a political party did not have any influence on that. And I speak very frankly when I say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Yes. And explain to the Judges how you know about what the SDS knew about and their activities during that time period. Explain how you know what was going on within the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was a member of the municipal board of the SDS. So whatever was happening in that party during that period of time, I had to know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And in fact, in 1991, you had been appointed one of the assistants to the then SDS president, Mr. Srdic. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not one of his assistants. I was a member of the municipal board of the SDS, and the SDS president did not have assistants. And I believe that the municipal board had 15 members or so. I can't say that with any precision. However, members of the municipal board of the SDS were the presidents of the local SDS boards, and certain other people, together with presidents of the local SDS boards.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, the vice-president of the SDS at the time of the takeover was who?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the period when the power was taken over, the vice-president was Dragan Savanovic. But they changed very often. I'm not sure. There were very frequent shake-ups among the top ranks of the SDS, within a very short period of time, to be very precise, within one year, there were three different presidents of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Well, in fact, the vice-president -- perhaps you're confused about the time period. But aren't you aware that Milomir Stakic was in 1992 the vice-president of the municipality in the Serbian democratic party, the SDS, in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, what period are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Well, do you know that Milomir Stakic was the vice-president of the SDS? Are you aware of the fact that he was at one time the vice-president of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of that. If he was, then that must have been later when I was no longer active in the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges, going back to your knowledge of the events, you were also appointed to a position as a negotiator for the SDS on interparty relations. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it isn't correct. I did not participate in the interparty relations agreements. There were other people appointed on behalf of the SDS who were in charge of political talks and the talks among the parties that existed at the time and that had seats in the assembly of Prijedor Municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: In fact, sir, do you know someone named Mr. Tursic? I believe you mentioned him during your direct examination as the head of the revenue department.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know the name Tursic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: In fact, weren't you responsible to negotiate on behalf of the SDS and Mr. Tursic on behalf of the SDA? Wasn't he your counterpart?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we didn't negotiate. I never negotiated with Mr. Tursic on behalf of the SDS. However, because of the nature of Mr. Tursic's work and because of the nature of my work, we had meetings, contacts. We had to talk.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Can you tell us, do you know the fate of Mr. Tursic?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Just for the record, I refer Your Honours to page 3102 of the book of missing persons. Sir, were you appointed at one time to a commission regarding gymnasiums with a Dr. Rufat Suljanovic?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you please repeat your question. I did not quite understand one word in your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, were you appointed to participate in a committee with Dr. Rufat Suljanovic? Do you know that gentleman?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was never a member of any committee or commission, and I do not know the name of this gentleman.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did the assembly ever appoint you to do anything -- to any commission regarding the schools?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, this was not within the authority of the assembly. The work with schools was not within its scope. My secretariat was the secretariat for economy and social affairs, and one of the -- the part of the social affairs were also schools. So the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor did not need to issue any particular conclusions or orders with regard to schools because it was under the authority of the secretariat of economy and social affairs under the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I would like the usher to hand the witness, first the Court and Defence, a document, it's an article from Glas dated the 17th of January, 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The article in Glas would be marked provisionally S391.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And for the record, it is, of course, the article on the left-hand side with the -- indicating the date line Prijedor, 16th January.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, if you could take a look at the B/C/S, at the actual article, on the left-hand side, not the top one, but the one farther down, beginning about the middle of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. We have an article translated on the 17th of January, so I just want to make sure we have the same article, because counsel referenced the 16th of January.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: The date for the newspaper is the 17th, and the date line of the article is the 16th. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Just tell me when you've read the article, sir. Sir, is the information in that article regarding your appointment accurate?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The article is a bit ambiguous. After the multiparty elections in Prijedor, I was proposed as a candidate for the post of the secretary for economy and social affairs. And here, the journalist speaks in very general terms. On the other hand, I started working in the municipality in the month of March 1991, and this article was written in January. At the time when this article was written, I worked in a private company whose name was Mont Commerz, the company was based in Split in the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, I believe the article is referring to your political appointment within the SDS, and not your professional position. Were you appointed by the SDS along with Mr. Vujinovic, Branko Koncar, Dragan Mikanovic to assist Mr. Srdic at that time?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] Excuse me, maybe we should clarify first which article the witness read. Interpretation [Interpretation] Which article did you read, sir? Could you perhaps read the title.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "The press made them smart." That's the article that I read.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, were you appointed along with the following individuals that I just named: Mr. Dusko Vujinovic, Branko Koncar, and Dragan Mikanovic, to assist Mr. Srdic by the SDS when he was the president of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The information carried by the media, or this particular journalists, and I don't know who the journalist is, this has been misinterpreted by the media. This information is wrong, and it was carried wrongly by the media. I never assisted Mr. Srdic, nor was I ever appointed a member of any commission. What the journalist wrote here is simply a misinterpretation of the information that he may have received from the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Actually, Your Honour, I see that we have under a different ERN a better copy of the article in which the name of the journalist is quite clear. Perhaps that could be substituted. I believe this article may already be marked, Ms. Karper informs me, as SK15. Perhaps someone could check. But I'll move on to another subject in the interest of time. And we can have the ELMO moved away for now. Thank you. The usher can take the article.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, would it be correct that you were a candidate for the SDS for the Municipal Assembly in the 1990 elections?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not during the elections, but after the elections.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: No, my question is, were you on the list of candidates for the assembly, the SDS list of candidates, for the assembly for the 1990 elections, for the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Believe me, I'm not familiar with that. I'm not familiar with having been on the list for a deputy for the Municipal Assembly. I don't know that I was on any list. It would be contrary to the rules which say that a head of a secretary cannot be a deputy in the Municipal Assembly. I repeat once again: Under the law, officials on the Executive Board cannot at the same time be either candidates or deputies in the Municipal Assembly. Therefore, I don't believe I was on any such list.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll move on, and perhaps come back to this later. Who was the candidate for the SDS party? Who did the SDS party nominate following the results of the elections for the position of vice-president of the municipality of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the elections, the multiparty elections, that is, after the interparty agreements, the SDS and the people's radical party proposed Dr. Stakic as the president of the Municipal Assembly. He was a member of the radical party.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Can you tell us the difference between the platforms of the SDS party and the radical party of Dr. Stakic?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Frankly speaking, I was not much into politics; therefore, I was not familiar with the platform of the radical party.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. When Dr. Stakic came back as the president of Prijedor, do you recall when that was when he came back into office at the end of the war as the president?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot give you a precise answer, but I believe that it was in early 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Who nominated Dr. Stakic as the candidate or as the new president of Prijedor at that time?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that because I left the SDS in January 1993. I was not politically active as a member of any party after January 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. That's fair. Sir, can you tell us why you were -- first, when you were removed from your position as a member of the Executive Board in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was somewhere around mid-April 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Well, following the takeover -- perhaps I'm a little confused. Did you have the same position at the time that the government of Prijedor was headed by President Cehajic as you did after the takeover of the municipality and Dr. Stakic became the president of the Serbian Municipality?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that the nature of my own position was a bit peculiar, and it's a bit difficult to understand perhaps. I'll try to keep this as concise and clear as possible in order to explain to you my situation, position, and my role in the Executive Board. In March 1991, as I told you, I was appointed the secretary for the economy and social affairs. However, there was an interparty agreement. There was no interparty agreement about the head of the communal services because a consensus could not be reached. There was a conclusion by the Executive Board in April 1992 appointing me to two different positions at the same time. So I kept my position as the secretary for the economy and social affairs and member of the Executive Board, and the Executive Board also appointed me the acting head of the communal services in Prijedor. After the takeover, as both these positions were very demanding, I opted for the latter. I opted to remain the head of the communal services. And Mr. Ranko Travar, who had a degree in economics was appointed to the position of the secretary of the economy and social affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir, that clarifies things. Can you tell us, sir, from your position as head of the communal services, is it correct that you were removed from that position in September of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I remained in that position until January 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: So you left that position the same time that Dr. Stakic left his position as president. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was in January. Municipal administration organisation, my secretariat as an organ of the municipal administration was within the purview of the Executive Board. And in that month, the president of the Executive Board resigned in writing, which meant that the whole of his team followed suit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us, sir, a little bit about the SDS party. You mentioned you were a member of the main board in Prijedor. First, do you know Dusan Baltic? Was he a member of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do know Dusan Baltic. He worked as the secretary of the municipality for a period of time. And then for some time, he was the head of the communal services. And frankly, I do not know that he was a member of the SDS. During the time that I was a member of the municipal board of the SDS, Mr. Baltic certainly was not a member of the SDS. I remained in that position for a very short time, and it may have been the case that Mr. Baltic did become a member of the SDS after that, but I do not know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. As a member of the main board in Prijedor, did you receive instructions, that is, the main board in Prijedor, from the republic level and regional levels of the party? In other words, did you ever receive instructions from Banja Luka or from Sarajevo or Pale and the higher leadership regarding the policies that should be followed in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've said, I was a member of the SDS, and for a short while, I was a member of the municipal board of the SDS, not, as you say, of the main board, because that is the republican level. In a municipality, you have municipal boards. All the correspondence down the vertical line between the municipal boards, across the municipalities, and the main board at the level of the republic, was within the purview of the party president. Therefore, I can't tell you anything more specific about such documents because I never laid eyes on it, nor was I aware of its contents; only the presidents knew about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Is it correct that in January of 1992, the party, the SDS party, formed a parallel government in Prijedor to which you were appointed?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think one could call this a parallel government. Even after that appointment or - what should I call it? Due to the failure of the government at that time to operate properly, this was a second option in a manner of speaking. But I still remained a member of the Executive Board, and I remained in all the positions that I had been discharging up to this point in time, up to the establishing of what you referred to as the parallel government. The one in place was not operating properly. I think this happened in January 1992; and after that particular date, the Executive Board continued to operate as before.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. I would be happy to use your terminology. This option 2 that you talk about, was this something that was under the -- according to the instructions received from the main board of the party that in Prijedor, there would be a separate Serbian government formed?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must go back to previous parts of my testimony, and I have repeated this a number of times. During the period that you refer to in your question, January 1992, I was not a member of the municipal board. I told you that I was member of that board for a very short time, at the beginning of 1992. If I may be allowed to continue, so I'm not familiar with who the instructions came from, whether from Banja Luka or from Pale, as you said. But I was not in a position to obtain this sort of information not being a member of the Executive Board.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I really apologise, but I think that we should clarify the year the witness just mentioned, because the interpreters entered it wrongly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I don't believe so. We were talking about the creation of the second option in January 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Is that correct? I think that's what I was talking, and that's what the transcript reflects that you answered concerning the creation of the second government in January 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But when he was the member of the municipal board, because I believe that the witness mentioned 1991. But you can clarify it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. But I understand the witness saying he was not a member of the main board in January 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, sir, Mr. Dragic, you can correct me if I am wrong. You told us you were not a member --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We shouldn't confuse main board and municipal board.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: You were not a member of the SDS municipal board in Prijedor in January 1992, but you were appointed to this second government, this option 2 government, in January 1992. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. I was not a member of the municipal board, but I was appointed member of the Executive Board, not a member of the government. But yes, that is some sort of municipal government.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And after being appointed to this position on the Executive Board, you never asked whose instructions it was or no one ever told you under whose instructions this option 2 government was formed. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At this time, it was not really an interesting issue, because the government did not do anything much. The government which was officially appointed to the assembly after the multiparty elections was in place. So this was not anything particularly interesting for us, and none of us were interested -- none of the members of the the new government were interested in this because the government was appointed, but it never operated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. I'm going to try to keep moving on. The position that you did have as the head of communal services, I believe - correct me if I have the title wrong - as part of that position, did you supervise the 4th of July company?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that you may find the internal organisation of organs and administration and communal services difficult to understand, because here, in the western world, this kind of organisation is not used, is not widely used. What you asked me about, the 4th of July, it's a public, state-owned enterprise for providing communal services, or to provide further explanation, we are talking about garbage collection and garbage dumping and sewer maintenance. So that's what the 4th of July provided, this sort of service. And the -- as an organ of municipal administration, my own section had different competencies, so there were no points of contact between these two legal persons. The only thing that was the case is that the communal institutions sometimes commissioned certain tasks to be carried out by the 4th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you finished with your answer? I didn't mean to cut you off. Thank you. Among the tasks that the 4th of July was given, did you give them the task of collecting dead bodies during 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, the communal institution or myself, as the head, we never even -- it never even occurred to us, nor were any of us in a position to issue such orders. The commissions that were handed out to the 4th of July was the maintenance of public areas and parks. So we are talking about general utility services. If there was a lot of rain, for example, the 4th of July would be put in charge of cleaning the streets. But this was the only thing we needed them for, and these were the only tasks that were given to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, you indicated that you served for a while with the then JNA, and you have some familiarity with that army. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Can you tell us, did you hear at that time if the JNA was the fourth largest army in Europe?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what people said, but personally I did not quite believe that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did you believe based upon your experience that the JNA was a professional and well-organised army?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My experience before the war, long before the war, ten years before the war, there would be military drills under the law of national defence, and military-aged men were to respond to callups for these military drills. And this was an opportunity for each military-aged man to get acquainted with the equipment and the -- that the JNA had at that time and the way things worked.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Let me be more specific. In Prijedor in 1992, was there a professional, well-armed -- were there elements of a professional, well-armed army in the municipality, specifically the 343rd Motorised Brigade manned by Colonel Arsic, and the Kozarac light Brigade commanded by Colonel Colic?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Before the war, across the former republics, every municipality had military garrisons or military barracks. Prijedor municipality had a barracks too, and the name of that barracks was Zarko Zgonjanin. Now, according to a certain structure that they had, it had the name, the 343rd Brigade. I know that before the war, before the war broke out, the commander of the barracks was Mr. Arsic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Was that brigade well organised, well armed, and commanded by professional soldiers, professional officers?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not exactly a military expert, you know. When I look at a structure within the military or a weapon or a equipment, I'm not qualified to say whether they were well organised or not and run in a competent way. Only military experts can provide you with an answer to this. I can only say that once I had completed my military service, my specialisation was still as a communications officer. But I was not -- I was never in a position to look at their equipment, the equipment they had within the barracks, so that I could be well placed to tell you about the quality or quantity of their equipment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think it's an appropriate time for a break now. The trial stays adjourned until quarter past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. For the transcript, we are proceeding with the full composition of the Bench, with three Judges. Mr. Koumjian, please continue. Before we forget, we have still this document S391. Objections related to this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: First, did the registry have time to check, is it SK15? Is it the same?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, it is SK15. But the English version may be tendered now as SK15B and SK15A.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: As usual. May I just have a look at it, please. In fact, it was admitted into evidence as SK15, and from that copy you can read that the author of the article admitted into evidence at that time is Rade Mutic. And as proposed, we take the English translation as SK15A. I can see no objections. Admitted into evidence. So please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, for the registry and also so Ms. Karper can perhaps prepare, I would also like in a moment to show the witness a document that's SK12. It's a very long document, and the particular page would be page 00916417 in English. I haven't yet located -- excuse me, Ms. Karper did locate the B/C/S page. And we will be able to tell you that. While she is preparing that -- here it is. I'm sorry. The B/C/S page is 01021618. Before I show the witness that document, though, perhaps I can avoid it by asking the witness to look at SK11. If that article can be shown to the witness. That's SK11. If there are not enough copies for the Defence, they can have mine. If the Defence needs a copy, they can have mine if no others are available. For the record, the witness appears to be reading the article, SK11.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Could Prosecution please switch off microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, just let me know when you're ready. Thank you, sir. Have you read the article and do you recognise it as an article by Zivko Ecim in Kozarski Vjesnik?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the first time I've laid eyes on this article, and I've read through most of its content.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: First, the person named in the article as the president of the SDA commission for negotiations, Mehmed Tursic, is that the individual that you talked about in your direct examination as the head of the tax department?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And this article indicates that Mr. Tursic was told that you were the president of the commission on negotiations for the SDS party. And then you are quoted in the article as saying: "Although you didn't know about the decision referred to in the article as a member of the party, you respect all of its conclusions." Sir, I have another document that's rather long. Let me just describe it, and if necessary I can show it to you. But it appears to be handwritten minutes of a meeting of the SDA party. I'm referring to SK12, the English page 00916417. And on the B/C/S, 01021618.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: If counsel would like a copy, they don't have it, we have a copy we can hand out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, in these minutes, it indicates that an interparty cooperation committee was proposed. The Chamber, the first name listed is Milovan Dragic. Does the article and what it just told you, would that remind you that you were asked by the SDS to negotiate with the SDA party?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said at the beginning, I was not a member of that commission. It's easy to realise if you look at this article in which this is also confirmed by Mr. Meho Tursic. He says: "In the meantime, I found out that Milovan Dragic was the president of the commission, and Blank pages inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Pages 10484 to 10489. when he wanted to verify this information, he found out that I was on vacation." But later on he found out that I was not what he had been told I was. I'm not sure if the translation is correct. And if I may add, it's clear from Mr. Tursic's statement that he had been under the wrong impression. He had obviously been given information that I was president of some sort of a commission, but that also later he found out that I, in fact, wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. I'm going to move to different subject matter. Thank you. Can you tell us, sir, you indicated you were appointed to the Executive Board. Can you tell us at that same time, was Mr. Drljaca appointed as the chief of police? I'm talking now about your by appointment by the SDS to the option 2 government, as you called it.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: While I was in the SDS, Mr. Drljaca was not on the Executive Board. While I was a member of the Executive Board, Mr. Drljaca was not the chief of the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I believe -- I'll come back to that in just a moment. Sir, let's move on to a different topic for a moment. You talked about Muslims and Croats leaving Prijedor, and I believe you indicated that many of these -- much of this was in response to the mobilisation. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we are talking about the year 1991, Muslims were leaving on a large scale by buses from various locations in Prijedor Municipality, and it was an organised thing. The real truth about their departure is hard to know. At the sessions of the Executive Board at the time, it was a very frequent item on the agenda. And the question was asked: "How come that Muslims were leaving the municipality, and they were leaving -- those who were leaving were women, children, and elderly people. In other words, those who were not military-aged and fit for military service. Since Mr. Mehmed Cehajic [as interpreted], the president of the municipality, was present at every session, Mr. Kovacevic would ask him that. He was the president of the Executive Board, and he would ask him that, and he would ask for the reasons for which these people were leaving Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may interrupt, we have to clarify it now. It's very important. The witness said the president of the Municipal Assembly. It's translated the president of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I hear comments from the booth, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction. What the counsel said is correct. The interpreter apologises.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you for the intervention, Mr. Lukic. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: You said, sir, that there were daily departures, and I am referring to page 26 of the LiveNote of yesterday, of these people by buses. And depending on the day, there were two or three or even more buses departing Prijedor Municipality on a daily basis. That's at the end of page 26 and the start of page 27. You told us this continued during the period from July through December 1991. Were these buses, just to give us an idea, did they appear to be buses that carried about 50 people? Would that be accurate?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly what types of buses were those. But it is a well-known fact that bigger buses have up to 50 seats. And let me continue what I started a minute ago. The departure from Prijedor --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Well, I'll just ask you to answer the questions. If you feel it's necessary to complete the answer to the question I asked, you may, but I think you answered my question. Can you tell us, then, would it be accurate that there were -- based on your estimates, I understand this is an estimate -- about a hundred people leaving per day?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: So in your estimate, if we say for that six-month period, 180 days, that would be 18.000 people leaving the municipality? You asked us to do the math. It's pretty simple. Is it correct that the population of Muslims in the municipality according to the census 1991 would have been just over 49.000?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct that up to the end of 1991, over 20.000 non-Serbs left Prijedor. And this information could be given to you in a more accurate form by those who were in charge of the transportation. When I say over 20.000 people, this is based on the daily departure of non-Serbs. What everybody was confused about, including the civilian authorities in the Executive Board, is the fact that Prijedor was being left only by those people who were not fit for military service, that is, women, children, and the elderly people. There were suspicions that something was being prepared, and those suspicions later on proved to be correct. Members of the non-Serbian ethnicity were leaving Prijedor during the time when there were no armed conflict anywhere in Bosnia and Herzegovina. There were no rebellions or any similar incidents. Non-Serbs were leaving Prijedor after the beginning of conflicts in Slovenia and especially after the beginning of war in Croatia. Prijedor is geographally very close to the Republic of Croatia. It is only about 30 kilometres away from the border of Croatia. In late 1991, there were a lot of refugees, Serb refugees, who came to Prijedor from the Republic of Croatia, and people were telling stories about what had happened in their places back in Croatia. And this instilled fear among the population of Prijedor. People were afraid that the situation that had prevailed in the neighbouring Republic of Croatia would somehow reach Prijedor. Unfortunately, it did happen in that way, and the conflict spread on to Bosnia as we know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. My question actually dealt with the census, and you went beyond that. If you can confine your answers to the questions, we can finish a bit quicker. You also explained yesterday that part of the fear that you had and the surprise that you had regarding these preparations for a conflict by the non-Serbs was due to a video that you saw. And the transcript indicates that you said that in 1991, foreign journalists came to Prijedor. Mr. Kovacevic organised a press conference in which this was shown. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: So this was part of the atmosphere of fear among the Serbian people prior to the takeover of Prijedor by the Serbian authorities in April of 1992. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fear was always present before the takeover as well as after it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: But you indicated that this video was a shock to you and other Serbs, and you indicated that this was shown following a visit of foreign journalists in 1991. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct. It is correct that the president of the Executive Board organised a press conference at which this video was shown showing the way Green Berets in Kozarac were preparing themselves for an armed conflict. I remember very well the two journalists from London turned their backs towards the screen when the video was -- started playing. I was surprised to see that. I was surprised to see that, but the president of the Executive Board reacted to that, to this reaction by the foreign journalists. They were two ladies who said "we are not going to watch this. We know that this has been edited, that it's just a fabrication." The other journalists who were present there watched the entire video.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Now, in response to this fear that you're talking about, did you participate in the plans for the takeover of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't participate. Even if somebody from the civilian authorities had wanted to participate, they couldn't, because it was not under their authority to do that. It was under the authority of the military bodies, the military bodies were the ones who were in charge of that. So even if somebody from the civilian side had wanted to participate, they couldn't. And let me add something else. I only learned on the 30th of April in the morning that Prijedor had been taken over.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Were you in Cirkin Polje very early in that morning with the -- with other persons who were planning the takeover?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, I wasn't in Cirkin Polje.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: So if any civilian leader gave a statement indicating that they had participated and coordinated with the army and the police in the takeover, that would be false?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the question. I'm afraid I didn't understand you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We are not allowed to ask this line of questions, so I don't think that the Prosecution should be allowed to ask it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Maybe there is an absolute misunderstanding. There was an intervention by one representative of the Prosecution saying that the parties would not be allowed to put these questions. But there was no ruling from the side of the Chamber in this way. So therefore, dismissed. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, you indicated you didn't understand, so I'll restate the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, you didn't allow me to ask Mr. Sivac these kind of questions. You ruled on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: In fact, I did, after a restatement. Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, from what you've told us, you didn't know anything. You didn't participate with the army. You weren't in any meetings - correct me if I am wrong - with Mr. Arsic; you weren't in meetings with Mr. Drljaca. Is that correct? Or were you part or party to any meetings in which the army or police planned the takeover of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I have just told you, I stand behind that. On the 29th of April, 1992, I was sitting with Mr. Mirza Mujadzic in the Prijedor Hotel. We dined together. We had dinner together. And after dinner in the Hotel Prijedor, together with Mr. Mirza Mujadzic and Mr. Sivo Saric, we went to the Europa restaurant in Prijedor, and we stayed there until very late in the night. On that occasion, I talked to these gentlemen about the situation in Prijedor which means that the question that you have just put to me, whether I was in Cirkin Polje, you can maybe call Mr. Mujadzic. And he can maybe tell you whether what I'm telling you is indeed true.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: My question is after you left the dinner with Mr. Mujadzic, did you go to Cirkin Polje and see Slobodan Kuruzovic, Milomir Stakic, and other leaders?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't go. That is what I have just told you in response to your previous question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: At that dinner with Mr. Mujadzic, was Colonel Arsic there?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the beginning for a very short time, for not more than half an hour all together.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: So on the night before you say the army took over power in Prijedor, Colonel Arsic dined with Mr. Mujadzic?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was in the evening hours in the Prijedor Hotel on the 29th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Was Simo Miskovic, at that time president of the SDS, present at that dinner?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, also for a very short period of time he was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Was Milomir Stakic there?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Now, this takeover, how were you informed of it?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I learned about that on -- in the morning, on the 30th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Just in regards to your knowledge of events both before and after the takeover, did you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt. Before you -- we missed the thread. How did you learn it in the morning of the 30th of April? Who informed you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I simply went to work in the morning. Actually, I went downtown, and I heard it when I got there that there had been a takeover.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You heard it from whom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was the talk of the town already when I got there. So I can't really remember who was it who told me first that it had happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did you see any posters regarding the takeover?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't see any posters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did you hear any announcements on the radio as to who was taking power?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't listen to the radio on that morning. I only listened to the media, watched television, when I got home after work in the evening. That's when I listened to the news.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: At that time, on this very important day in Prijedor, who do you recall -- what announcements do you recall regarding who was taking power in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. There were no announcements. If there were any, I don't remember them. I believe that the population was informed by the media. I believe it was announced on the Radio Prijedor maybe, but I didn't listen to the radio on the morning hours of that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did you hear Dr. Stakic speaking after the takeover? And I'm not just talking about that morning, but in the following days and weeks, did you hear Dr. Stakic speaking on the radio?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I listened to the radio only rarely. I watched television mostly. But I can't remember that I heard Dr. Stakic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: So when the military took over, did Mr. Arsic become the president of the municipality or how did you see that the army had taken over Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was nobody else to do it but the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: To your knowledge, did the SDS play any role in the planning, preparation, and the carrying out of the takeover of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You've already asked me that, and I've told you that as far as I know, the SDS did not plan anything with regard to the takeover of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to move on now for a moment to Mr. Drljaca. When did you first meet Mr. Drljaca?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew Mr. Drljaca before the war. Mr. Drljaca liked to play indoor football in his free time, so we would meet when we played tournaments. My acquaintance with Mr. Drljaca is quite long. We go way back before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Was Mr. Drljaca -- would it be accurate that before becoming the chief of police in Prijedor was an administrator for the schools? He was an individual with a law degree who worked as an administrator for the schools in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know that Mr. Drljaca had a degree in law and that he worked in the centre for primary education in Prijedor. Yes, he discharged some administrative duties, but I don't know exactly what duties those were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I have a document I'd like distributed. I do not believe it's in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: If I could continue questioning the witness, it may not be necessary to use the document. We could cut down on the paper. It could be given to the counsel and the Court right now, and just hold off with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, who appointed Simo Drljaca as the chief of police in Prijedor? Sorry, maybe you didn't hear the question. Sir, Mr. Witness --

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I heard your question. But I'm not in the position to know who appointed whom. I can only tell you what the then prevailing law on state administration provided for. And when it comes for the police, what was provided for by the law was that the chief of the police or the chiefs of the public security stations and centre for security were appointed by the Ministry of the Interior at the republican level. And as I already told you this yesterday, what I did had nothing whatsoever to do with the police, so I really don't know who appointed Mr. Drljaca to the position of the chief of the public security station in Prijedor. However, according to the provisions of the law, this is done by the Ministry of the Interior, its competent bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, perhaps I was confused. So is it correct, then, that you don't know how the police functioned in fact in Prijedor in 1992? You have no information about that. All you can tell us is what's written in the law.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that the police functioned according to the law, like it did before the armed conflicts in the 1980s. It continued to function in the same way in the 1990s.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, let me have you take a look, then, in this document which is marked in English as 03024765, and in your language, our number is P0038604.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: This would be provisionally S391.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, do you recognise this document as a ballot paper for members of the executive committee in which both your name as the candidate for the director of the public utilities company and the name of Simo Drljaca as the candidate for chief of the public security station appear?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with this document. According to this paper, the deputies of the Municipal Assembly would have had the right to vote. But I was not a deputy. This is a list for members of the executive committee of Prijedor municipality. And the only ones who had the right to vote were the deputies in the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor. And as I've already told you, I was not a deputy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: All right. Is it correct that you were appointed by this assembly to the position of director of public utilities company as shown on this ballot paper?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. Here it doesn't specify which assembly we're talking about, from which period.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, I want to go back to the fear you talked about that motivated the takeover. I believe you testified last -- on your direct examination that there was fear of a Muslim plan to take over Prijedor and to commit again what had happened in World War II. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say that there was a fear of the takeover in Prijedor by non-Serbs. What I said was that there was fear among the population, fear of an armed rebellion and of an armed attack. This was -- the fear was not about who would be in power; it was fear of armed rebellion. The political leadership of Bosnia and Herzegovina ordered the local bodies across the municipalities in Bosnia and Herzegovina to attack the barracks. And it was a well-known fact that 95 per cent of the people there were Serbs. So that was an open order, you could say, that was issued to attack Serbs in the municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, who was this order issued to? Who was going to attack the JNA at that time in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This order came from the presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and the president at this time was Mr. Alija Izetbegovic. The order in writing came from the Ministry of the Interior of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: My question is who it was directed to --

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And the minister --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Let me repeat the question. Who was the order directed to? Who was supposed to attack the JNA in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The order was addressed to the political leadership of the SDA in Prijedor. And the order was signed by Mr. Alija Delimustafic. I can tell you exactly what the order said if you would like me to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I would like you to first tell us this, sir: Did you really take seriously that there was a possibility that someone would order the Muslim forces, whatever they were in Prijedor, to attack the JNA and the 343rd Motorised Brigade, a professional armoured unit in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I took the order very seriously. And those who made the decision or gave the order must have taken it even more seriously in Prijedor. If you say the 343rd Brigade, the name itself suggests that it includes a great number of people, of manpower. But you must know that those people were not in Prijedor. According to the law, people responded to the mobilisation callup, which means that they were outside Prijedor Municipality. In the Zarko Zgonjanin barracks itself in Prijedor, the only people remaining there were security officers and a small number of the reserve forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, Ms. Karper has informed me that the document I've just shown the witness is already marked as S262.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, were the Serbian people, and particularly the SDS, arming themselves prior to the takeover? Were arms being distributed by the party or by the army to Serbs in Prijedor Municipality?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No one gave Serbs in Prijedor weapons. Serbs responded to the mobilisation callup, and there was no need for anyone to give them weapons. Only those people who responded to the mobilisation got the weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, did you ever attend any meetings of the Crisis Staff in Prijedor? I'm not asking if you were a member; did you attend any meetings of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did you attend any meetings of the Prijedor National Defence Council? Just so we're clear about the translation, I'll read the title in your language: Narodnu Obranu Skupstine Opstine Prijedor. Did you attend any meetings of that organisation?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understood your question. You asked me about the National Defence council, but I was not a member of that council. So there was no need or possibility for me to attend its meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Just so we're clear, I'm not asking whether there was a need or possibility. Your answer, as I understand it, is you did not attend any meetings of that body. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: So, sir, can you tell us based upon your limited knowledge, who ordered the attack by the army on villages and the cleansing of villages in Prijedor Municipality? Under whose orders and in coordination with what bodies did those attacks take place?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Attacks on villages. Can you specify? There are lots of villages surrounding Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you, that's a fair question. Let's start with the 24th of May and the attack on Kozarac, the surrounding villages, Kamicani, Kozarusa, Jakupovici. Those villages were attacked on the 24th of May. If you disagree, you may tell me so. Can you tell me who ordered those attacks and with what bodies they coordinated?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The attack was carried out by the army. And naturally, the army had its own commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And was anyone in the municipal government, to your knowledge, informed about these attacks before they occurred?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not know that anyone from the municipal government was informed about that. Not as a person, not in my capacity. The army never notified the bodies of civilian authority about the actions it was about to take, and the law on national defence did not envisage that they should have.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. If we could now distribute S110. We have extra copies for those who do not have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like you to just look at the headings, and then direct yourself to Article 6. You told us yesterday that the civilian authorities had no influence on mobilisation.
