Having read over this Article 6, can you see that in the third paragraph, the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor clearly authorises the Crisis Staff to consider issues of mobilisation, development, and reinforcement of the armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know what you're saying. This is the Official Gazette of Prijedor Municipality. What was published in it is that at its session of the 25th, the Assembly adopted a decision on the organisation and work of the Crisis Staff. What is written here is true. This must have been said at the assembly, and that's why it was then carried by the Gazette. However, in practice, on the ground, none of these things could be applied for the simple reason that the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor, looking at the whole thing from a legal point of view, how legal something was, the Municipal Assembly was at a lower level than the law itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay, I understand you're not a lawyer, so I don't want to debate the law with you. But is it correct that your position, then, is that the Crisis Staff was illegally given power?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't read this thoroughly, so it's impossible for me to conclude that the Crisis Staff was actually empowered. I worked in the Executive Board at this time, and I did not notice the Crisis Staff being there at all. Because the executive power was still in the hands of the Executive Board. I should go through this more thoroughly and be given more time to read it, and then perhaps I'd be able to comment on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, did you attend the session of the assembly on the 20th of May, 1992, in which this was adopted?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not a deputy, and it was not my obligation to attend any of the sessions, which in fact includes this particular one. Sessions are attended by deputies, or persons specifically invited by the president of the assembly. This included in the agenda a decision would be adopted by the assembly concerning a particular legal person or legal institution, and then such persons as affected by these decisions would be specially invited, but aside from these cases, no other persons attended the sessions of the assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: So who was this person -- you said that the president had the authority to invite persons to the sessions. Who was that person in May 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The president of the assembly. That was Mr. Stakic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: The article indicates, Article 6, indicates that among the duties of the Crisis Staff, second to last, is keeping abreast of all aspects of the situation in the municipality essential for the waging of armed combat and take appropriate measures. Do you have any information that this was not done?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This article, what you've just read, I think there may have been a small error in the interpretation, or perhaps the lady interpreter. The text of the Serbian original is keeping abreast of all aspects of the situation in the municipality and all elements essential, and this means keeping abreast with the elements essential for the waging of armed combat. It just says "keeping abreast," keeping informed. And that's how the translation should read. So the Crisis Staff is familiarized with the essential elements but does not order or coordinate anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, do you know who set up the detention camps in Omarska and Keraterm in the Prijedor Municipality?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first reception centre was set up in Trnopolje, and immediately after the war events in Kozarac, that's when it was set up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues]... because I didn't ask you about Trnopolje. I asked you about Omarska and Keraterm. Please try to limit your answer to the question. Do you know, if you don't know, say so, who set up these detention camps?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The army did because persons were being interrogated in those premises, and the interrogations were done by the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did you ever see any orders to arrest any individuals or to refuse the release of any individuals from these camps?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry, I have once again to interrupt. Mr. Dakic, in case you don't know, please tell us. From the transcript, it reads now that "the persons were being interrogated in those premises, and the interrogations were done by the army." How can you come to this testimony? How do you know that it was the army? You are under solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll answer your question in the following way: I know that it was done by the army because my closest colleague in my institution, the one I worked in at that time, the public works, he was working there as a lawyer, Pero Tadic, a very close colleague. He had been mobilised by the army, and he received orders as a lawyer to carry out interrogations of persons in the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Do you know who saw the interrogations, the results of those interrogations, the statements that resulted?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not familiar with that. The results of interrogations are not known to me, the number, not the results, after the interrogations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: So, sir, correct me if I am wrong, but if you were to discover information that a civilian leader had known about the takeover prior to it happening, had participated in arming Serbs in preparation for -- arming Serbian civilians in preparation for a conflict, had set up camps in Omarska and Keraterm, and had given demands to many of these villages to surrender weapons before they were attacked and warnings that they would be attacked, then your whole impression as to the power of this civilian and his role in controlling events in Prijedor would change. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to my knowledge, the calls to surrender weapons were sent by the army to the civilian population of those villages. And those who complied with this demand, and those were many, turned over their weapons at the Zarko Zgonjanin barracks. The fact itself that those civilians who were in possession of weapons decided to go to the barracks and turn over their weapons there implies and leads you immediately to the conclusion that they were responding to a demand made by the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: But if you saw an article that was signed by the Crisis Staff demanding that those weapons be surrendered that appeared in Kozarski Vjesnik, you would change your opinion. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't read that particular article. I was not familiar with that. What I've just told you about the army being the only one to call upon people to hand over their weapons was also due to the fact that those who did have weapons had nowhere else to turn them over but at the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: On the 30th of April, 1992, the army in Prijedor was the JNA. The VRS, army of Republika Srpska, the VRS, had not been formed. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember the exact date. However, the JNA was present in Prijedor Municipality until, I think, mid-May 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Do you recall the reaction of President Cehajic when this option 2 government was formed that you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This government was only formed on paper. It was a paper tiger. It never actually operated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: But do you recall the reaction of President Cehajic to the announcement of this government?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I can remember his reaction or what he stated. I know that they kept opposing, or in other words, they failed to implement the law on national defence which was punishable under the law. But none of the politicians, including Mr. Cehajic, were ever made to answer for that. If the law had been more strictly complied with, they would have been made to answer for their actions before a military court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Well, what happened to Mr. Cehajic? You said he did not answer for this. What did happen to him?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: On the executive committee, you worked with Becir Medunjanin. Do you know what happened to him?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Medunjanin for a while, he was a member of the Executive Board, and we used to meet at meetings. We all had -- we both had our own area of activity, and the only contacts we had were during the meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: That wasn't my question --

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what became of that gentleman, whether he's somewhere abroad or wherever.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like to show you a --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like to now show you an issue of Kozarski Vjesnik from the 28th of April, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: It's S47.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: In the interests of time, I'm going to read portions of this to you, and ask you to comment. If you feel it necessary to read the whole article, say so. In the second paragraph, the second sentence: "By nature, an unobtrusive but determined and tenacious man, Stakic, still deputy chairman of joint municipal assembly in Prijedor, came to realise that the SDA and HDZ are contriving a plot to get rid of Serbs, and he used every opportunity to counteract them." Did you observe Dr. Stakic using every opportunity to counteract the SDA and HDZ prior to the takeover?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't find this sentence, but regardless of that, I will answer your question. I know Dr. Stakic, and what the journalist says here is not something that one would regard the way his personality was. On the contrary. I don't know who the author of this text is, and which paper that is from. But I believe that I know Dr. Stakic better than the journalist who wrote this article, and that for that reason, my opinion of Dr. Stakic is more credible. And my opinion is just the contrary of what the opinion of the journalist is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Well, what do you disagree with? Do you believe Dr. Stakic was -- the description is unobtrusive, but determined and tenacious. What do you disagree with?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is very generalised. What does it mean, determined? What does it mean tenacious, in what?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: You indicated that you have the opposite view. So I'm asking you, why do you disagree with this?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't agree because I know Dr. Stakic better than any journalist, regardless of who it is. But in any case, these atributes that this journalist attributed to Dr. Stakic, these are not the characteristics of his personality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, you know Dr. Stakic better than any journalist. You know him very well. You don't know that he was president of the Crisis Staff in Prijedor in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that this is -- this is beyond comparison. I don't think these two pieces of information cannot be compared. I didn't say journalist, but the journalists who have signed this article, and the signature of this article is Mr. Rajcevic, and I think, it is my claim, that Mr. Rajcevic doesn't know Mr. Stakic very well. He knows him just as an acquaintance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry. I'm absolutely tired of you trying to circumvent the questions. The question was you don't know that Dr. Stakic was the president of the Crisis Staff in 1992. Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: This is your final testimony, that you did not know that Dr. Milomir Stakic was president of the Crisis Staff in the town where you worked.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We will discuss the consequences of this answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to go on to a few paragraphs, the paragraph beginning with a dash. It's on the left-hand side, left column, the last paragraph. I will read slowly. You can read along with me. It indicates that this is the words of Dr. Stakic, what he said at the start of the interview. "What happened on the 30th of April, 1992, was only the final act of a long-standing, but for the Serbs, perilous plan. I often talked in private with the leaders of the SDA and HDZ, and this is what convinced me that they were concocting a terrible plan regarding the Serbs. They were secretly arming themselves, making uniforms with the symbol of the lily, building strongholds in Kozara and the neighbouring districts. But we were not just sitting there with our hands in our laps. When we saw what they were doing, we began to arm ourselves and to tell the party members what they were planning to do to us, and what has to be done to prevent 1941 from happening all over again. On the direction of the central office of the SDS, we formed the Serbian Assembly of Prijedor, and I became chairman. When I arrived to work the next day, the then chairman of the joint assembly, Muhamed Cehajic, greeted me with the following words: "Hello, colleague. Now we are both chairmen, and I congratulate you from all my heart and wish you success." But in spite of his smile, I knew what was behind those words and what they were planning to do to us." Is this consistent with statements you heard Dr. Stakic make in 1992 and afterwards?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot confirm whether this was said to the journalist by Dr. Stakic. I am not familiar with this interview. I don't know of this interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: That wasn't my question. You said you knew Dr. Stakic. You also were a member of the SDS party. Is this consistent with what you heard Dr. Stakic saying in 1992 and afterwards?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know Dr. Stakic, I can say about one part of this text that may have been said by Dr. Stakic. I cannot claim that for a fact, but I can assume that some of that may have been said by Dr. Stakic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: If Dr. Stakic indicated that the Serbs were arming themselves and preparing, would you change your opinion now and -- about whether or not Serbs were being armed by the SDS party prior to the takeover?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already said in my answer to one of the previous questions that the Serbs did not need to arm themselves because they responded to the mobilisation call by the army, and they got the weapons from the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Well, then, if I now understand your answer, you're telling us that the army gave weapons to Serb civilians. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never said civilians. I said that Serbs did not need to arm themselves because they responded to the mobilisation calls, and they were given weapons by the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Well, men in the army were given weapons. Were men outside of the army given weapons? Were men allowed to take their weapons after they left the army?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Army members until mid-May 1992 were members of the Yugoslav People's Army. And they were allowed to, in case they went home for a short rest or break, they were allowed to take weapons with them because in order to get to their houses from the front line, they had to move through unfamiliar areas and war-struck areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: So I gather from the beginning of your answer that you now remember that on the 30th of April, the army was still the JNA. You indicated earlier you didn't know when the transformation took place.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that I said that I did not know the date of that transformation, but that that transformation took place in the beginning of May of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: So you now know that on the 30th of April, 1992, the army in Prijedor was the JNA. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, judging by the date, it was still the JNA, and the difference between the JNA and the army is not big. The same people stayed in the same places. Only the insignia on the uniforms changed, so it was very difficult to be very precise about the date of the change because there were no major changes as such. People were the same, but the only thing that changed were the insignia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: In May of 1992, where did Dr. Stakic live?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Well, in fact, didn't Dr. Stakic live in Omarska and have an apartment in Prijedor and travel between the two?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When you asked me where he lived, I said in Prijedor. In Prijedor, there are local communes, there are streets. You have to put me a precise question. You should have asked me in which local commune he lived. I told you he lived in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: You got me there. I'm sorry. I apologise. Did he live in Omarska or in the town of Prijedor in May of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't give you a precise answer on the time frame. It has been ten years, but I know that he lived in Prijedor. I don't know in which month that was. I can't give you a precise answer on the month where he lived there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: In May 1992, did you travel through Kozarac after the attack on Kozarac, in May or June of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I told you yesterday was that my journey from Banja Luka was via Kozarac, but the road was blocked by military equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. But I'm asking after the 24th of May. I think on direct, you made it clear that was before the 24th of May, but correct me if I am wrong. After the attack on Kozarac on the 24th of May, did you travel through Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Through Kozarac, can you be please more precise. When you say "through Kozarac," when you travel from Banja Luka to Prijedor, you have to pass through the local commune of Kozarac, but you stay on the road. If you want to enter Kozarac, you have to get off the road in order to enter Kozarac. Can you please be more precise. Can you please ask me if you want whether I travelled on the road via Kozarac, or did I actually enter the local commune of Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. I was referring to the main road. Did you see the destruction of Kozarac after the 24th of May from the main road?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the main road, obviously you could see the degree of damage because the houses there are in the immediate vicinity of the road, so one could clearly see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And can you briefly describe what Kozarac looked like from the main road.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was damage on the family houses there, on the -- on other buildings. There is a mill. There is a community house which was damaged. Some family houses were damaged. And then a part of the mill which is very close to the road itself was also damaged.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: By the way, you mentioned some international issues. Are you aware that on the 22nd of May, 1992, Bosnia was admitted into the United Nations?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that Bosnia was admitted, but I'm not sure about the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I want to continue with the article, and you may read along with me. "In April, things started to happen in Sarajevo, Bosanska Krupa, and other places. This convinced us that we have to speed up the process of arming ourselves. All the more so, as on the 6th of May of that same year, Muslims and Croats called an all-party conference inviting managers of various firms and prominent people, formed their government, appointed heads of SUP as well as heads of army and other institutions. I was informed through my own channels that a decision had also been reached to take over power by force. We were lucky that Colonel Arsic was the commander of our garrison, a soldier and a man with a lot of experience. And we decided that we must speed up the process of arming ourselves." Sir, who do you understand Dr. Stakic to mean when he says "we decided that we must speed up the process of arming ourselves"?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is hard to draw any conclusions based on this paragraph that you have just read. It's hard to conclude what Dr. Stakic actually meant. It's hard for me to say what he meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. Continuing: "An interesting thing happened on the 20th of May, Stakic continued. When travelling to work from Omarska, I saw in Prijedor, in Kozarac, armed Muslims with lilies on their sleeves. I noticed the same in Kozarusa, and I knew that the time for action had come." Sir, what do you believe Dr. Stakic means in this article when he says, "I knew that the time for action has come?"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I interrupt. I think the time has to be balanced between the parties. And we can't see the priority that is given by the Prosecution putting an article and ask for the opinion on an article to the witness. Therefore, may we ask the OTP also to come to an end of their questions. And I don't know what is -- what is the area, other areas? We should try to end the line of questions put to the witness by the Prosecution about 6.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll try to do it sooner than that. I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: During your statement just recently, you said, "I knew Dr. Stakic better than any journalists." Later you [indiscernible] this a little bit. But could you please tell us since when you knew Dr. Stakic and what was your relationship with Dr. Stakic?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I met Dr. Stakic in the first part of 1991, during the first three months of 1991 when I came to the municipality. And when I took my office of the secretary for economy and public affairs. At that time, Dr. Stakic was the vice-president of the Municipal Assembly. Mr. Stakic is some ten years younger than me, so we are not the same generation. We are not as close as we otherwise could be if there was no generation gap between us. And not only that, there is a generation gap between us, but also my job and things that I did, job, and things that Dr. Stakic did were two different things. I have a degree in economics; Dr. Stakic is a physician. So we could not get together through work. We first got acquainted in the month of March 1991, during the first three months of 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So your testimony is you didn't meet him in -- earlier in 1991. It was March, actually March 1991. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. I knew him by sight from the time of the multiparty elections which took place during the last three months of 1990. So to be more precise, I saw him for the first time in the year 1990, during the last three months of 1990. I didn't know him before that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: When you discussed on pages 27, 28 of today's transcript that what you called "option 2," as from January 1992, one question was left open: Was this option 2 a plan caused by the disagreement with the work conducted in Prijedor itself so that one could argue it was a specific solution for Prijedor, or was it based on the recommendation, order, whatsoever, from a higher level?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I said in my testimony that it was like a reserve option or option 2, I had in mind the functioning of the civilian authorities in case that this functioning was the way -- or the nonfunctioning was the way it was in -- under the circumstances of division between the Serb ethnicity and the Muslim ethnicity. I told you there was a 50/50 ratio in the executive branch of the government based on ethnicity. In a certain way, the decision on setting up this second option government was more like a warning that the Serbian population of Prijedor Municipality, in case the nonfunctioning of the executive branch of the government continued, would be forced to have its own parallel form of government. And that is what I meant when I spoke about this second option or reserve option.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: But still the question is: Was a specific Prijedor solution emanating from the needs as you may have seen them for Prijedor, or was it part of a more general solution in former Yugoslavia? Specifically, did people, others than representatives of Prijedor, participate in the meeting in January 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understood your question. It was a local issue. And it was an issue very specific to Prijedor, as you have put it. There were no people from other municipalities present at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: When you went to work the 30th of April, 1992, which office did you enter, the same as the day before or another one?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't go to my office. As usual, every morning before we went to work, we would have a coffee in a nearby coffee place, and this is where I learned of the events of the previous day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Is it correct that the 29th of April, you worked in the secretariat for economic and social affairs?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: In which capacity did you work the 30th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 30th of April, I worked in the same capacity. I was waiting for the newly appointed person, Mr. Ranko Travar, to take over from me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: How did you know that there was a newly appointed person?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Prior to the 29th, I believe that there was a decision - I can't remember exactly whether that was a decision of the Executive Board or a decision by the Assembly. I can't remember. I don't remember which body issued that decision, whether it was the Municipal Assembly or the Executive Board. There was a decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: When did you start acting in your new capacity - forgive me if I quote it in the wrong way. I think the correct name was director of public utilities company.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember the exact date. Nothing much changed in my work for all intents and purposes. It was only about how my work was described, the title. Instead of acting director, I said director of the public utilities. As I told you at the beginning, I was working on two different things at the same time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We have an extremely short break now just for the exchange of the tapes. For technical reasons, we will continue and try to finalise the testimony today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May it be part-time work or the entire work, when, for the first time, one could read at your door or you got the document that you were now appointed director of the public utilities company?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember the date. But I think it was in May 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Previously, you were shown Document S262, a ballot paper for members of the executive committee and secretaries of the departments of the Serbian Assembly of Prijedor Municipality. The candidates appearing on this list, and one of them, number 9, was you. Were they asked beforehand whether or not they were prepared to exercise this function if elected?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, before a person would finally be appointed, certainly those who had proposed the nomination would have talked to that person and asked them if they were ready in case they were elected by the assembly to assume the position. I believe this was common practice. And that's how the president of the Executive Board would always go about it. Because after all, it was the president of the Executive Board who choose his own colleagues and people he worked with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: This brings me to the next question: Could you please tell us in terms of hierarchy who were your superiors following the 30th of April, 1992, in the hierarchy, please?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as my superiors were concerned, there was only one person who was my superior, and that was the president of the Executive Board, Mr. Milan Kovacevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Would it be a wrong assessment that the takeover in January 1992 was more or less an implementation of that what was planned in January 1992 because some persons came to the assessment that it was necessary to have a functioning -- to have functioning organs in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it is my personal conviction, and I think I'm not mistaken, the events that occurred in January 1992 did not indicate that what it was about was so to speak the first phase of a takeover. What happened that at least was my conviction was aimed at warning the partners in government, or more specifically, the Muslims, about the degree of seriousness requested for discharging civilian affairs. In practice, there was a lot of negligence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think we have understood this. Can you tell us the reason why you left SDS in January 1993 apparently in a close timely connection with your resignation, the resignation of Dr. Stakic, the resignation of Dr. Kovacevic?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My reason for leaving the SDS was of a personal nature. When I say personal nature, I mean that I was not in agreement with how the party ran affairs related to personnel issues. And when I say "affairs related to personnel issues," I'm convinced that mistakes were being made in that sense and that certain positions in certain companies or institutions were in my opinion filled by the wrong people. When I say "the wrong people", I'm only referring to their professional qualifications and their experience.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you agree that you worked in the fields of the economy and social affairs between 1992, 1993?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Secretary for the economy and public works, I worked in that capacity until the first days of the month of May 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And that's when I became the director of public utilities. And I left that position in January 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. You had the opportunity to have a glance through the Official Gazette of Prijedor Municipality dated the 25th of June, 1992 where we can read the decisions of 20 May 1992. In Article 7 it reads: "In exercising its functions from the fields of the economy and social affairs, the Crisis Staff shall in particular adopt decisions relevant to the organisation and functioning of the economy in the public, private, and mixed ownership sectors, the organisation and functioning of social affairs, the organisation and management of finance sector, and the care of refugees and the destitute." As a civil servant, you had to obey the law. You had to obey the rules. When were you confronted the first time with Article 7 of this decision on the organisation and work of Prijedor municipal Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Honestly, I've seen it here for the first time. And I am surprised when I look at the text that I have read here today for the first time, because I still remember the time, the period of time we are discussing. I'm talking about May and the end of 1992. The public utilities worked from May 1992 on just like it had functioned before. Nothing changed about the way it operated. And really, I understand this may strike the Honourable Chamber as strange that in that particular capacity, I did not have a chance to read the Official Gazette. But believe me, those who were in charge of delivering copies of the Official Gazette to all public companies were quite negligent in their job sometimes. And I'm here referring to the secretariat of the municipality because they were the ones who were in charge of furthering copies of these important documents to other people and other institutions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues]... Mr. Dusan Baltic?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dusan Baltic. Dusan Baltic was the secretary of the municipality. I can't remember when he stopped being the secretary, but the things I told you about, forwarding copies of the Official Gazette and that sort of thing, definitely the secretary and his own administration would have been in charge of these chores.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So it is your testimony that you never received any kind of orders, recommendations, under Article 7 of these rules on Crisis Staff as I just read out?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never received any written documents from the Crisis Staff, such as orders, decisions, or conclusions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: What about oral orders, decisions?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not oral either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Is it your testimony that you never read Kozarski Vjesnik or an Official Gazette where articles or decisions were signed by Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've already said, I did occasionally read Kozarski Vjesnik, but when these particular decisions you're referring to were published, no, I did not read those particular issues. I hardly ever bought Kozarski Vjesnik. Those were local papers also during the war. And when you do buy your own copy, you look at the announcements and ads.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So it remains your testimony finally that you never heard about the existence of a Crisis Staff in Prijedor. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not what I said. I didn't say I never heard of its existence. I said I had heard of its existence, but in my work, I did not feel it operate, nor did I know where its seat was, where its offices were. I worked with those people in the Executive Board with whom I had also worked before the decision on the establishment of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you ever visit Dr. Stakic in his office in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were visits. I can't give you the exact date, but yes, there were visits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Was Dr. Stakic or another person you saw at the corridor in uniform or armed?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. It was translated in Serbian: "Dr. Stakic or somebody else."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: That was the question. Or somebody else on the same corridor. This was the question. Was Dr. Stakic or any other person you saw on the corridor in uniform or armed?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the corridor or in the office, in the municipal building. For a while --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: First, on the first question, did you see Dr. Stakic in his office in uniform?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did see Dr. Stakic in uniform, but if you want me to specify in answer to your question whether that was in his office or maybe outside the building itself, I can't specify because I can't remember. But I did see Dr. Stakic wearing a uniform. It's just that I can't tell you whether it was the corridor, the office, or the office. I can't recall exactly, but yes, I did see him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Finally, what was the reason you had to visit Dr. Stakic in his office?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I visited the president of the Municipal Assembly when Dr. Cehajic was the president, and also when Dr. Stakic was the president. It was just something I did in my spare time. They would have me over for a cup of coffee, for tea. We would share a drink. The nature of my work was not really related to their work, the work done by the different presidents of the assembly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: When you were there for a cup of coffee or tea, did you discuss politics, problems related to the SDS?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as we were sitting there, we were not silent. That's for sure. We were talking. But our conversation did not focus on politics. Dr. Stakic as the president of the assembly was more interested in potential problems of my institution, the institution that I headed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you ever ask him why suddenly he wore a uniform?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't ask him that. Members of the Executive Board wore uniforms too, but only for a very brief while. I think not -- for no longer than a week, seven days. There was no need to ask them individually because other members wore uniforms too, other members of the executive power. That's what I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: But not you yourself.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did. I did too, for a short while. When I was the director -- as the director of a municipal -- as an organisation of municipal administration, we had to act in the general spirit and not on the basis of our individual decisions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And what was this general spirit?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think you have misunderstood. I was referring to the uniforms. If the other members of the Executive Board were wearing uniforms, I did not wish to be an exception to this rule. I did not want to stick out as an individual. I just wanted to play along with the rules.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think I have understood your answers. Judge Vassylenko.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: I would like to ask you the following question: You knew very well Milan Kovacevic. He was your superior. You knew Ranko Travar and Vojo Pavicic. They were members of the Executive Board, as you testified before. How often have you met those people before the takeover and after the takeover?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Prior to the takeover, Mr. Ranko Travar did not work in any bodies of administration, and he was not a member of the Executive Board of Prijedor Municipality. He came later, after the 30th of April. Mr. Vojo Pavicic had indeed worked as a member of the Executive Board prior to the 30th of April. And the remaining members of the Executive Board, Radenko Banovic and all the others, after the 30th of April, my contacts -- after the 30th of April, my contacts to other members of the Executive Board were the same as before. The nature of my work in the public works required frequent visits to the building of the Municipal Assembly just to take care of the current affairs there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: And those people, they never told you that they are members of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we didn't talk about it. Those were younger people, and we didn't talk about it, and they didn't tell me anything about that specific issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: And they never acted in capacity of member of Crisis Staff while talking with you, while answering your question, advising you something, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were in no position to advise me. I was their senior, and I had more experience in exchanging such duties. So if anything, it would have been the opposite.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Judge Argibay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Yes, please, I want to focus on two or three points that I'm a little bit confused about. And I am not wrong, and I am quoting from the top of my head, yesterday you told us that you never were a part of a commission or a committee or some sort of working group, let's say, in your capacity as a member of the Executive Board or prior to that as a member of the SDS. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a member of a working group of some coordination body, on behalf of the Executive Board, yes, I was. But I was never a member of any commission on behalf of the SDS or any body of the SDS. So that means operatively, yes, but no political appointments in that sense.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, this is clear. Can you tell me which working group were you part of as a coordinating body on behalf of the Executive Board? What was the fundamental subject of this working group?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Due to the nature of my work and my position as the director of the institution, one of the activities of the institution was drafting plans for -- drafting urban -- drafting plans for urban planning in the town. A five-year platform would be drafted, and then this platform consisted of yearly plans within this period of five years. When drafting such plans, by virtue of my position, and not only by virtue of my position, I did work together with other members of the Executive Board on drafting those plans. Not all the members of the Executive Board were included, only those whose activity was related to the nature of the plan being drafted. And I'm talking about two specific secretariats, the secretariat for urban planning, housing affairs, and property affairs, and the land surveys office and cadastre office.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: In that capacity, in that working group, you had the secretariat for urban planning, housing affairs, property affairs, land surveying affairs, and all that. Did you take care of the housing and allocation of refugees that came into Prijedor as far as we know since 1991 onwards?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Among other things, part of my institution's work was to run state-owned flats and administer state-owned flats, but I didn't have any specific obligation to do anything about refugees. When I say managing state-owned flats, I mean maintenance and investment related to housing facilities and shared housing facilities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Okay. I'll change the subject, please. You were telling us that the 343 or 43 Brigade of the JNA in Prijedor, in the barracks in Prijedor, was a very small brigade because all the people were out fighting in the war or something. How could this brigade of the JNA take over Prijedor if they had such a small amount of people at their disposition?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You didn't need a huge manpower to take over power in Prijedor, as in addition to members of the army, members of the reserve force of the police also participated in that. The takeover occurred in a completely nonviolent way, not a single person was shot or wounded. So it didn't really take that many people. There are only several buildings holding the civilian bodies. In Prijedor, as in any other town, you had the municipal building, the police headquarters, and the distance between all these buildings was not that great. They were usually up to a hundred metres away from each other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: But then there's the thing I can't understand. You told us also that before the takeover, you knew about a -- I think you called it the Green Beret army being formed in Kozarac if I'm not wrong, and then that it was a very big army with a lot of arms and things you seen from your car, and then in a video. And then these people didn't appear at all against a small portion of soldiers of the JNA on the takeover of Prijedor? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Green Berets and Kozarac is some 12 kilometres from the town of Prijedor, so the Green Berets were not in the town, and they didn't prepare themselves in town, but in their local commune.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: I think this would be the last question. You said something about this group preparing rebellion against the Serbian population. Would you say that the takeover by the army against elected civilian authority was an act of rebellion? And please answer yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN DRAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Any further questions by the parties?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We don't have any questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: None due to the time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. This concludes your testimony. You're excused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The trial stays adjourned until tomorrow. And in this case please rely on this information: 1.30 to 15.00, 15.30 to 17.00, 17.20 to 19.00 in Courtroom I.
